title: Weak hadith and virtue
hookLine: scholars differ on using weak hadith for encouragement, never for law

cards: A card on a fridge door, held up by a magnet. On it, a gentle saying about kindness to neighbors, and underneath: the Prophet ﷺ. Nobody in the house remembers where the card came from.
Is the saying sound? Weak? Made up by someone with good intentions?
Suppose a report is weak, but all it does is urge people toward something good. May it be used at all? Scholars have answered that differently, and both answers are worth hearing.

teach.h: WEAK IS NOT THE SAME AS FALSE.
teach.b: First, what weak means. A weak report, da'if in Arabic, isn't necessarily false. The chain or the text fell short: a narrator with a poor memory, a gap where a name should be.
The critics simply can't vouch for it. Then, the line drawn around law.
In this discussion, weak reports were kept away from questions of what is permitted and what is forbidden; law needed firmer ground. Then the disagreement.
Some scholars allowed a weak report to be mentioned to encourage a good deed that already stands on sound texts: giving charity, being patient, remembering Allah. Tradition says they set conditions.
The report must not be very weak. The deed must already be grounded elsewhere. And the speaker must not claim with certainty that the Prophet said it.
Other scholars refused weak reports altogether, even for encouragement, holding that the sound reports give more than enough. Last, why both sides cared so much.
In the introduction to his Sahih, Imam Muslim records a report that whoever narrates something from the Prophet that he sees to be a lie is one of the liars.
And Sahih al-Bukhari carries the Prophet's warning against anyone who lies about him on purpose.
So both sides guard the same thing: one by keeping doubtful reports at arm's length, clearly labeled, the other by keeping them out of the room.
You can hear the care in the wording some scholars used: not the Prophet said, but it is reported. A small change of words, and an honest one.

how: Muslim teachers differ on whether weak reports may be recited to encourage good deeds; those who allow it often signal the doubt with wording such as "it is reported", and weak reports are not used to establish law.

games.q: what does “weak hadith and virtue” mean?
o: whether a report critics can't vouch for may urge good deeds
the rule that weak reports may settle what is lawful
a made-up saying that teaches people how to be good

games.q: weak hadith and virtue — tap the pairs.
p: weak: the critics can't vouch for it
careful wording for a doubtful report
whoever narrates a lie is one of the liars

s: a weak hadith means a made-up one
weak means the critics can't vouch for it: a gap in the chain, a narrator with a poor memory.
scholars who allowed weak reports used them to settle what is lawful
weak reports were kept away from law. some allowed them only to encourage a deed already grounded.
Imam Muslim's introduction warns against narrating a saying you see to be a lie
whoever does it, the report says, is one of the liars.

games.q: you've heard a moving report, graded weak, that urges people to give in charity. you're about to share it with friends. what do you do?
o: share it as "the Prophet said", since the message is good.
if you share it at all, say "it is reported", and lean on sound texts for the point.
add a line or two to make it stronger.
games.why: the scholars who allowed weak reports asked for exactly this care, and other scholars would leave it out entirely. neither side would present it as certain.

practice: Bring to mind a line you've repeated as someone else's words: a quote you posted, a saying you credit to a parent, a teacher, a prophet. Do you actually know where it came from?
Without scolding yourself, rest a moment in the small gap between he said and it's said that he said.

wordCard.voice: Weak hadith and virtue. Whether a report the critics can't vouch for may be used to encourage good deeds: some scholars allowed it with conditions, some refused, and they kept it away from law. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: weak. used of a report whose chain or text falls short of the standard.

carryVoice: Your line: careful with the weak. Not the Prophet said, but it is reported. See you tomorrow.
